title: Allocation-size overflow and defensive allocation patterns (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or control flow.
Recognize common failure and safety cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Before allocating count elements of size element_size, the program must ensure the multiplication count * element_size is representable in size_t. If count exceeds SIZE_MAX / element_size, the multiplication would wrap and request too little storage.
understand.whyItMatters: An undersized allocation followed by indexing according to the original count can cause a buffer overflow. Defensive allocation validates arithmetic before requesting storage.
understand.analogy: Treat each resource and operation as having a clear contract, valid lifetime and failure path.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the C standard, compiler or library specifications.

explain.narrative:
Before allocating count elements of size element_size, the program must ensure the multiplication count * element_size is representable in size_t. If count exceeds SIZE_MAX / element_size, the multiplication would wrap and request too little storage.

Check object bounds, lifetimes, arithmetic limits and all relevant return values. Compile with warnings enabled and test both normal and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The division check proves that count multiplied by element_size will not exceed SIZE_MAX. The helper then requests the calculated number of bytes.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why checking the result after multiplication is too late if the multiplication already wrapped.
practise.independentTask: Write an allocation helper for a two-dimensional array and validate both multiplication steps.
hints: Include stdint.h for SIZE_MAX where provided by the implementation and use size_t for sizes.
Handle zero elements according to a documented policy.
Check additions as well as multiplications when calculating header-plus-payload sizes.
